about: Every number here was measured by the ts-r project and recorded in a commit message, a crate's AGENTS.md, a design record or bench/README.md. Each section says what was measured, on what machine and project, how many runs, the command that reproduces it and the commit that recorded it. Pre-alpha: only the pieces that exist today are measured, and the numbers that miss their targets are shown too. Lower is better unless a chart says otherwise.

machines.mac: Apple M-series Mac, macOS arm64, release build (the exact chip was not recorded)
machines.unrecorded: Not recorded with the result. ts-r's measured runs so far are on the project's Apple M-series development Mac (macOS arm64, release build).
machines.laptop: Apple M-series MacBook (macOS arm64, 16 cores, 48 GB), shared with other jobs while measuring; release build, 4 threads
machines.review: Linux x86-64: four cores of the review box's bench machine, a cpuset nothing else is scheduled on while it measures (one bench slot); release build. The CPU model is not recorded with the result

projects.three-x10: mrdoob/three.js src copied ten times (the bundler benchmark esbuild and Bun publish), pinned in bench/repos.toml

sections.title: ts-r-dev against Vite 8 on excalidraw
sections.intro: excalidraw (about 500 TypeScript modules served from source, 47 dependency entries) served by ts-r-dev and by Vite 8.3.4 with @vitejs/plugin-react 6.1.2. Start is process spawn until the canvas and welcome screen are in the page; cold means an empty ts-r cache and no Vite dependency cache. Both kept React state through all 53 edits with 0 full reloads. SCSS is replaced by an empty stylesheet for both servers (ts-r-dev does not compile it yet).

sections.intro: Time from saving a file to the browser having re-imported the changed module and run its callbacks, on generated apps. The plan's target is under 30 ms at p50, staying flat as the project grows. Vite has not been measured on these generated apps yet.

sections.title: ts-r-build against esbuild 0.28.2 on a dedicated Linux machine

Both bundlers produce the same exports from the same input. Without its persistent cache ts-r-build took 962.9 ms against esbuild's 1,409.8 ms; with the cache, 484.6 ms. The shared-laptop runs below are older (commit 2fb2555), and there the two were level without the cache. Peak memory and excalidraw were not measured on this run.

sections.title: ts-r-build against esbuild 0.28.2 on the shared laptop
sections.intro: Bundling two public projects on the shared laptop, with older code than the Linux run above: three.js x10 (ten copies of three.js, minified IIFE with source maps) and the excalidraw app (minified ESM). Only three.js x10 is drawn as bars: both bundlers produce the same exports from the same input. At commit 2fb2555, without its persistent cache, ts-r-build was about as fast as esbuild there: three invocations of 10 runs each gave medians of 231.8, 233.9 and 255.0 ms against esbuild's 262.7, 238.5 and 246.2 ms, so esbuild was faster in the last one, which the bars show. On excalidraw ts-r-build does less work than esbuild: it does not bundle template-literal import() yet, so it leaves out the 61 locale chunks esbuild emits (7.2 MB of output against 9.3 MB). Those runs, the single bundle and the 20 rebuilds, are in the table with that note, not drawn next to esbuild. Rolldown and Vite's production build have not been measured.

sections.title: ts-r-lint against ESLint with the same rules
sections.intro: tRPC's own ESLint config with every rule ts-r-lint does not implement removed, given to both tools as the same file, on the same 147 files: 48 rules, without type information on either side. Both report 0 problems from those rules. The bars are the run where ts-r-lint evaluates the config in Node every time, as ESLint does; most of its time is that Node process. By default ts-r-lint caches the evaluated config and then takes 15.5 ms, but ESLint has no such step to skip, so that run is in the table, not drawn next to ESLint. With type-aware rules the runs are not comparable yet: on tRPC ts-r-lint's parity gate turns those rules off (its type check reports one error tsc 7 does not), and with the gate off it reports 11 problems ESLint does not.

sections.title: ts-r-check against tsc 7.0.2 on a dedicated Linux machine
sections.intro: The check scenarios the review box runs on every pull request, on four dedicated Linux cores: a cold check (no saved history) of three public projects against TypeScript 7.0.2's native tsc, from the bench of pull request #42 on 2026-10-24. These are the numbers in the README's benchmark table. ts-r-check reports exactly tsc's diagnostics on tRPC and date-fns, and on RxJS 6 extra and misses 5 of about 21,900 (2026-10-24, 087afc9); it also skips checks it does not implement yet, so these times will move as the checker grows. With its saved history and nothing changed it took 140.9 ms on RxJS, but 401.0 ms on tRPC and 1,020.4 ms on date-fns, about as long as a cold check there. TypeORM and Playwright are not in the review box's set, and peak memory was not measured on this run: both are in the shared-laptop run below, which is older.

sections.title: Ecosystem: the top 1,000 npm packages
sections.intro: cargo xtask ecosystem runs each stage that applies to a package and compares it with the reference tool. Pass rate is pass / (pass + fail + error); skipped packages have nothing to compare. The check stage imports each package with skipLibCheck off and passes it when ts-r-check prints the same diagnostics (file, line, column, code) as tsc 7; in the 57 packages that fail, 121 of the 1,460 compared diagnostics differ (119 that only ts-r-check reports, 2 that only tsc reports). The parse stage fails 30 packages on grammar errors that ts-r's parser reports in JavaScript files Node and tsc accept, most often TS1313 (an empty statement as the body of an if). Two of the four selected packages' own test suites pass with ts-r swapped in; the other two (chalk and commander) fail only on an extra TS2661 from ts-r-check, and pass with its errors ignored.
